A name given to similar compilations used in the Greek and Oriental churches.—'''Absolutions in the breviary.''' {{smaller|See ''absolution''.}}—'''Breviary of Alaric,''' {{smaller|a compilation of the written and unwritten laws of Rome, made by Alaric II., king of the Visigoths, {{sc|a. d.}} 506.}}

'''breviate†''', ''v. t.'' [< L. ''breviatus'', pp. of ''breviare'', shorten, < ''brevis'', short. Cf. ''abbreviate'' and ''breve'', ''v.''] To abridge. ''Sherwood.'' See ''abbreviate''.

'''breviate†, breviat†''', ''n.'' [< L. ''breviatus'', ''breviatum'', neut., pp. of ''breviare'', shorten: see the verb.] '''1.''' A short compend; a brief statement; a summary.
{{smaller block|I will give you a ''breviat'' of all that hath been spoken.
{{right|''Middleton'', Family of Love, v. 3.}}
The same little ''breviates'' of infidelity have . . . been published and dispersed with great activity.
{{right|''Bp. Porteous'', Charge to Diocese of London.}}}}
'''2.''' A lawyer’s brief. ''S. Butler.''

'''breviature''' (brē′vi-ạ-t̮ūr), ''n.'' [< ''breviate'' + ''-ure''.] An abbreviation. ''Johnson.'' [Rare.]

'''brevicaudate''' (brev-i-kâ′dāt), ''a.'' [< L. ''brevis'', short, + ''cauda'', tail.] Having a short tail; brachyurous.

'''Breviceps''' (brev′i-seps), ''n.'' [NL., < L. ''brevis'', short, + ''caput'', in comp. ''-ceps'' (''-cipit-''), head.] A genus of tailless amphibians, typical of the family ''Brevicipitidæ''.

'''brevicipitid''' (brev-i-sip′i-tid), ''n.'' A toad-like amphibian of the family ''Brevicipitidæ''.

'''Brevicipitidæ''' (brev″i-si-pit′i-dē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Breviceps'' (''-cipit-'') + ''-idæ''.] A family of firmisternial salient amphibians, typified by the genus
readings.c1s3:
¶
'''brevilingual''' (brev-i-ling′gwa̤l), ''a.'' [< L. ''brevis'', short, + ''lingua'' = E. ''tongue.''] Having a short or small tongue; specifically, of or pertaining to the ''Brevilingues'' or ''Brevilinguia''.

'''Brevilingues''' (brev-i-ling′gwēz), ''n. pl.'' [NL., pl. of ''brevilinguis'', short-tongued, < L. ''brevis'', short, + ''lingua'' = E. ''tongue.''] In Merrem’s classification (1813), a group of birds including the hoopoes and kingfishers, or the ''Upupidæ'' and ''Alcedinidæ'' of modern authors.

'''Brevilinguia''' (brev-i-ling′gwi-ä̤), ''n. pl.'' [NL., neut. pl. of ''brevilinguis'', short-tongued: see ''Brevilingues.''] In some systems of classification, a group of ''Lacertilia'', or lizards, comprising those with an elongated and sometimes snake-like body, a short tongue, and generally eyelids: contrasted with ''Fissilinguia'', ''Crassilinguia'', ''Vermilinguia'', etc.

'''breviloquence''' (brẹ̄-vil′ọ̄-kwẹns), ''n.'' [< L. ''breviloquentia'', < ''breviloquen(t-)s'', short-speaking, < ''brevis'', short, + ''loquens'', ppr. of ''loqui'', speak.] A brief or laconic mode of speaking. [Rare.]

'''brevi manu''' (brē′vī mā′nū). [L., lit. with a short hand: ''brevi'', abl. of ''brevis'', short; ''manu'', abl. of ''manus'', hand: see ''brief'' and ''manual.''] '''1.''' Offhand; immediately; without delay; at once.—'''2.''' At or by one’s own hand; without the intervention of another; specifically, in ''Scots law'', on one’s own authority, or without legal warrant.

'''breviped''' (brev′i-ped), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< L. ''brevis'', short, + ''pes'' (''ped-'') = E. ''foot.''] '''I.''' ''a.'' In ''ornith.'', having short feet.

'''II.''' ''n.'' A bird having short feet.
readings.c2s1:
¶
'''brevipen''' (brev′i-pen), ''n.'' [< NL. ''brevipennis'': see ''Brevipennes''.] A bird having short wings; specifically, one of the ''Brevipennatæ'' or ''Brevipennes''.

'''Brevipennatæ''' (brev″i-pe-nā′tē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., fem. pl. of ''brevipennatus'', short-winged: see ''brevipennate''.] A group of brachypterous or short-winged web-footed birds, the ''Brachypteres'' or ''Pygopodes'', including the penguins, auks, guillemots, loons, and grebes. [Not in use.]

'''brevipennate''' (brev-i-pen′āt), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< NL. ''brevipennatus'', < L. ''brevis'', short, + ''pennatus'', winged: see ''pennate''.] '''I.''' ''a.'' Having short wings; brachypterous; specifically, of or pertaining to the ''Brevipennatæ'' or ''Brevipennes''.

'''II.''' ''n.'' A bird having short wings.

'''Brevipennes''' (brev-i-pen′ēz), ''n. pl.'' [NL., pl. of ''brevipennis'', < L. ''brevis'', short, + ''penna'', wing: see ''pen''<sup>1</sup>.] In Cuvier’s classification of birds, the first family of ''Grallæ'', comprising the ostriches and cassowaries, emus, dodos, and didine birds, and the apteryx: an artificial group, but in the main the same as ''Struthiones'' or ''Ratitæ''.

'''brevirostral''' (brev-i-ros′tra̤l), ''a.'' Same as ''brevirostrate''.

'''brevirostrate''' (brev-i-ros′trāt), ''a.'' [< L. ''brevis'', short, + ''rostratus'', beaked, < ''rostrum'', beak.] In ''ornith.'', having a short bill.

'''Brevirostres''' (brev-i-ros′trēz), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < L. ''brevis'', short, + ''rostrum'', beak.] In Sundevall’s classification of birds, a synonym of his ''Cursores''.
readings.c3s2:
A house or establishment in which the operations of brewing are carried on.

'''brewing''' (brö′ing), ''n.'' [Verbal n. of ''brew''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.''] '''1.''' The act or process of preparing liquors from malt and hops; the process of extracting a saccharine solution from malted grain and converting that solution into a fermented alcoholic beverage called ale or beer. {{smaller|The process usually followed by the brewer may be divided into eight distinct parts, viz., the grinding of the malt, mashing, boiling, cooling, fermenting, cleansing, racking or vatting, and fining or cleaning.}}—'''2.''' The quantity brewed at once.
{{smaller block|A ''brewing'' of new beer, set by old beer, maketh it work again.
{{right|''Bacon'', Nat. Hist.}}}}
'''3.''' A mixing together.
{{smaller block|I am not able to avouch anything for certainty, such a ''brewing'' and sophistication of them they make.
{{right|''Holland'', tr. of Pliny, xiv. 6.}}}}

'''brewis''' (brö′is), ''n.'' [< ME. ''brewes'', ''browes'', ''brouwys'', etc., < OF. ''broues'', prop. pl., from sing. *''brou'', < ML. ''brodum'', gravy, broth, < OHG. ''brod'' = E. ''broth''<sup>1</sup>, q. v. Cf. ''brose''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1†.''' Broth; pottage.
{{smaller block|<poem>What an ocean of ''brewis'' I shall swim in!
{{right|''Fletcher'' (''and another'' ?), Prophetess, i. 3.}}
Thou for all
The kitchen ''brewis'' that was ever supt
Shalt not once dare to look him in the face.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Gareth and Lynette.}}</poem>}}
'''2.''' Bread soaked in broth or the liquor in which beef is being boiled; also, brown bread warmed in milk.

'''brew-lock†''', ''n.'' A brewing.
{{smaller block|<poem>I ne’er hurt their churnings,
Their ''brew-locks'', nor their batches.
{{right|''Middleton'', The Witch, i. 2.}}</poem>}}
readings.c3s3:
¶
'''brewster'''<sup>1</sup>† (brö′stėr), ''n.'' [< ME. ''brewster'', ''brewestere'', ''browstere'', a female brewer, also a (male) brewer, < ''brewen'', brew, + ''-ster''.] One who brews; a brewer; more especially, a woman who brews.
{{smaller block|He [the chemist] is not a ''brewster'' like another, but a man who adds new utility and value to every creature in the brewery.
{{right|''Spectator'', No. 3018, p. 575.}}}}

'''brewster'''<sup>2</sup> (brö′stėr), ''n.'' The sweet-bay, ''Magnolia glauca''. [New Jersey.]

'''brewsterite''' (brö′stėr-īt), ''n.'' [After Sir David ''Brewster'' (1781–1868).] A white, yellow, or green pellucid mineral of the zeolite family, occurring in short prismatic crystals; a hydrous silicate of aluminium, strontium, and barium.

'''breyd'''†, ''v.'' and ''n.'' See ''braid''<sup>1</sup>. ''Chaucer.''

'''breziline''' (brē-zil′in), ''n.'' [F. ''brésiline''.] Same as ''brazilin''.

'''brian''' (brī′an), ''v. t.'' [E. dial., perhaps for *''brine'', < ''brīne'', orig. a burning. Cf. ''brin''<sup>1</sup>, var. of ''burn''<sup>1</sup>.] To keep fire at the mouth of (an oven), either to give light or preserve the heat. [North. Eng.]

'''briar, briary''', etc. See ''brier'', ''briery'', etc.

'''briarbot''' (brī′är-bot), ''n.'' [< ''briar'', ''brier'', + (appar.) ''bot'', a var. of ''but''<sup>2</sup>.] A local Irish name of the fish called the angler. Several brier-like protuberances arm the head.

'''breviductor''' (brev-i-duk′tọr), ''n.''   [NL., < L. ''brevis'', short, + ''ductor'', leader.]   The short adductorial muscle of the thigh; the adductor brevis. [Rare.]

'''brevier''' (brẹ̄-vēr′), ''n.''   [So called from being used in printing breviaries; < G. ''brevier'', < F. ''bréviaire'', < L. ''breviarium'', a breviary: see ''breviary''.]   '''1.''' A size of printing-type measuring 112 lines to the foot, next larger than minion and smaller than bourgeois. The larger type of this Dictionary, as in the present paragraph, is brevier.—'''2.''' Figuratively, something smaller than another taken as a norm.   ''Coues'', Key to N. A. Birds.

'''breviflexor''' (brev-i-flek′sọr), ''n.''   [NL., < L. ''brevis'', short, + NL. ''flexor''.]   A short flexor muscle. [Rare.] See ''flexor''.—{{smaller|'''Breviflexor digitorum''', the short flexor of the toes. Also called ''flexor brevis digitorum''.—'''Breviflexor hallucis''', the short flexor of the great toe. Also called ''flexor brevis pollicis pedis''.—'''Breviflexor minimi''', the short flexor of the little finger or the little toe. Also called ''flexor brevis minimi digiti''.—'''Breviflexor pollicis''', the short flexor of the thumb. Also called ''flexor brevis pollicis''.}}

'''brevifoliate''' (brev-i-fō′li-āt), ''a.''   [< L. ''brevis'', short, + ''folium'', leaf: see ''foliate''.]   In ''bot.'', having short leaves.

'''brevi manu''' (brē′vī mā′nū).   [L., lit. with a short hand: ''brevi'', abl. of ''brevis'', short; ''manu'', abl. of ''manus'', hand: see ''brief'' and ''manual.'']   '''1.''' Offhand; immediately; without delay; at once.—'''2.''' At or by one’s own hand; without the intervention of another; specifically, in ''Scots law'', on one’s own authority, or without legal warrant.

'''II.''' ''n.'' A bird having short feet.

'''Brevipennatæ''' (brev″i-pe-nā′tē), ''n. pl.''   [NL., fem. pl. of ''brevipennatus'', short-winged: see ''brevipennate''.]   A group of brachypterous or short-winged web-footed birds, the ''Brachypteres'' or ''Pygopodes'', including the penguins, auks, guillemots, loons, and grebes. [Not in use.]

'''brevipennate''' (brev-i-pen′āt), ''a.'' and ''n.''   [< NL. ''brevipennatus'', < L. ''brevis'', short, + ''pennatus'', winged: see ''pennate''.]   '''I.''' ''a.'' Having short wings; brachypterous; specifically, of or pertaining to the ''Brevipennatæ'' or ''Brevipennes''.

'''II.''' ''n.'' A bird having short wings.

'''Brevipennes''' (brev-i-pen′ēz), ''n. pl.''   [NL., pl. of ''brevipennis'', < L. ''brevis'', short, + ''penna'', wing: see ''pen''<sup>1</sup>.]   In Cuvier’s classification of birds, the first family of ''Grallæ'', comprising the ostriches and cassowaries, emus, dodos, and didine birds, and the apteryx: an artificial group, but in the main the same as ''Struthiones'' or ''Ratitæ''.

'''brevirostrate''' (brev-i-ros′trāt), ''a.''   [< L. ''brevis'', short, + ''rostratus'', beaked, < ''rostrum'', beak.]   In ''ornith.'', having a short bill.

'''Brevirostres''' (brev-i-ros′trēz), ''n. pl.''   [NL., < L. ''brevis'', short, + ''rostrum'', beak.]   In Sundevall’s classification of birds, a synonym of his ''Cursores''.

'''brevity''' (brev′ị-ti), ''n.''   [< L. ''brevitas'', < ''brevis'', short.]   '''1.''' Shortness; especially, surprising or excessive curtailment of the thing spoken of: as, the ''brevity'' of human life. Specifically—'''2.''' Shortness in speech or writing; conciseness; condensation into few words.
{{smaller block|''Brevity'' is the soul of wit. {{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, ii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|This argument is stated by St. John with his usual elegant ''brevity'' and simplicity.
{{right|''Bp. Porteous'', Rel. Observance of Good Friday.}}}}
{{smaller|='''Syn. 2.''' Compression, terseness, pithiness, succinctness, condensation, sententiousness, curtness.}}

'''Brevoortia''' (bre-vör′ti-ä̤), ''n.''   [NL.; named after Mr. J. Carson ''Brevoort'', of New York.]   A North American genus of herrings, family ''Clupeidæ'',
characterized by the elongated intestine and carinated scales. {{smaller|''B. tyrannus'' is the well-known mossbunker or menhaden, formerly included in the genus ''Alosa'' or ''Clupea'' (''A.'' or ''C. menhaden''). See ''menhaden''.}}

[[File:century v01 p0703 c2f1.png|center|273px]]
{{c|{{smaller|Menhaden, or Mossbunker (''Brevoortia tyrannus'').}}}}

'''brew'''<sup>1</sup> (brö), ''v.''   [< ME. ''brewen'' (pret. ''brew'', later ''brewede'', ''brewed'', pp. ''browen'', later ''brewed''), < AS. ''breówan'' (strong verb; pret. *''breáw'', pl. *''bruwon'', pp. ''gebrowen''; found only in pp.) = OFries. ''briuwa'' = D. ''brouwen'' = MLG. ''bruwen'', ''browen'', ''bruen'', LG. ''brugen'', ''bruen'', ''brouen'' = OHG. ''briuwan'', MHG. ''briuwen'', ''brūwen'', G. ''brauen'' = Icel. ''brugga'' = Sw. ''brygga'' = Dan. ''brygge'', brew; prob. connected with L. ''de-frutum'', new wine boiled down, Gr. βρῦτον (for *φρῦτον), a kind of beer; the primitive meaning, as indicated by the (probable) derivatives ''broth''<sup>1</sup> and ''bread''<sup>1</sup>, being prob. more general, ‘prepare by fire,’ hence ‘boil, brew, bake.’ See also ''brewis'', ''brose''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To produce as a beverage by fermentation; prepare (beer, ale, or other similar liquor) from malt, or from malt and hops, or from other materials, by steeping, boiling, and fermentation.—'''2.''' To prepare by mixing, boiling, or the like; mingle; mix; concoct: as, to ''brew'' a bowl of punch; “drinks ''brewed'' with several herbs,” ''Bacon.''
{{smaller block|''Brew'' me a pottle of sack. {{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., iii. 5.}}}}
{{smaller block|A witch who ''brew’d'' the philtre. {{right|''Tennyson'', Lucretius.}}}}
'''3.''' To contrive; plot; prepare: as, to ''brew'' mischief.
{{smaller block|He ''brew'' this cursednesse and al this synne.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Monk’s Tale, l. 395.}}}}
{{smaller block|I found it to be the most malicious and frantick surmise, and the most contrary to his nature that, I think, had ever been ''brewed.'' {{right|''Wotton.''}}}}
{{smaller block|Or ''brew'' fierce tempests on the wintry main.
{{right|''Pope'', R. of the L., ii. 85.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To conduct the operations or the business of brewing or making beer.
{{smaller block|I wash, wring, ''brew'', bake, scour. {{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., i. 4.}}}}
'''2.''' To be in a state of preparation; be mixing, forming, or collecting; be impending: chiefly in the present participle: as, a storm is ''brewing'' in the west.
{{smaller block|There is some ill ''a-brewing'' toward my rest.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., ii. 5.}}}}
{{smaller block|From the appearance of the clouds a gale was evidently ''brewing.''
{{right|''Marryat.''}}}}

'''brew<sup>1</sup>''' (brö), ''n.''   [< ''brew''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'']   The mixture formed by brewing; that which is brewed.

'''brew<sup>2</sup>†.''' Obsolete form of ''bree'' (which see).

'''brewage''' (brö′ā̤j), ''n.''   [< ''brew''<sup>1</sup> + ''-age.'']   A mixed drink; drink brewed or prepared in any way.
{{smaller block|I’ll no pullet-sperm in my ''brewage.''
{{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., iii. 5.}}}}
{{smaller block|Some well-spiced ''brewage.''
{{right|''Milton'', Areopagitica.}}}}
{{smaller block|A rich ''brewage'' made of the best Spanish wine.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng., ii.}}}}

'''brewer''' (brö′ėr), ''n.''   [< ME. ''brewere'' (= D. ''brouwer'' = G. ''brauer''); < ''brew''<sup>1</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   One who brews; specifically, one whose occupation is the preparation of malt liquors.—'''Brewers’ grains.''' {{smaller|Same as ''draff.''}}

'''brewery''' (brö′ėr-i), ''n.''; pl. ''breweries'' (-iz).   [= D. ''brouwerij'' = G. ''brauerei''; < ''brew''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ery''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' A brew-house; an establishment in which brewing is carried on.—'''2†.''' Brewers collectively; the beer-trade.
{{smaller block|If they should bring any distress and trouble upon the London ''brewery'', it would occasion the making ill drink, and drive the people to brew themselves, which would destroy the duty.
{{right|''C. Davenant'', Essays on Trade, I. 79.}}}}

'''brewet†''', ''n.''   [< ME. ''brewet'', ''bruet'', < OF. ''brouet'', pottage or broth, dim. of ''brou'', broth, pl. ''broues'', > E. ''brewis'', q. v.]   A kind of pottage.

'''brew-house''' (brö′hous), ''n.''   [< ME. ''brewhous'' (= OHG. ''brūhūs'', G. ''brauhaus''); < ''brew''<sup>1</sup> + ''house.'']   A house or establishment in which the operations of brewing are carried on.

The quantity brewed at once.

{{right|''Bacon'', Nat. Hist.}}}}
'''3.''' A mixing together.
{{smaller block|I am not able to avouch anything for certainty, such a ''brewing'' and sophistication of them they make.
{{right|''Holland'', tr. of Pliny, xiv. 6.}}}}

'''brewis''' (brö′is), ''n.''   [< ME. ''brewes'', ''browes'', ''brouwys'', etc., < OF. ''broues'', prop. pl., from sing. *''brou'', < ML. ''brodum'', gravy, broth, < OHG. ''brod'' = E. ''broth''<sup>1</sup>, q. v. Cf. ''brose''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1†.''' Broth; pottage.
{{smaller block|<poem>What an ocean of ''brewis'' I shall swim in!
{{right|''Fletcher'' (''and another'' ?), Prophetess, i. 3.}}

{{right|''Tennyson'', Gareth and Lynette.}}</poem>}}
'''2.''' Bread soaked in broth or the liquor in which beef is being boiled; also, brown bread warmed in milk.

'''brew-lock†''', ''n.'' A brewing.
{{smaller block|<poem>I ne’er hurt their churnings,
Their ''brew-locks'', nor their batches.
{{right|''Middleton'', The Witch, i. 2.}}</poem>}}

'''brewster'''<sup>1</sup>† (brö′stėr), ''n.''   [< ME. ''brewster'', ''brewestere'', ''browstere'', a female brewer, also a (male) brewer, < ''brewen'', brew, + ''-ster''.]   One who brews; a brewer; more especially, a woman who brews.
{{smaller block|He [the chemist] is not a ''brewster'' like another, but a man who adds new utility and value to every creature in the brewery.
{{right|''Spectator'', No. 3018, p. 575.}}}}

'''brewster'''<sup>2</sup> (brö′stėr), ''n.'' The sweet-bay, ''Magnolia glauca''. [New Jersey.]

'''brewsterite''' (brö′stėr-īt), ''n.''   [After Sir David ''Brewster'' (1781–1868).]   A white, yellow, or green pellucid mineral of the zeolite family, occurring in short prismatic crystals; a hydrous silicate of aluminium, strontium, and barium.

'''breyd'''†, ''v.'' and ''n.'' See ''braid''<sup>1</sup>.   ''Chaucer.''

'''breziline''' (brē-zil′in), ''n.''   [F. ''brésiline''.]   Same as ''brazilin''.

'''brian''' (brī′an), ''v. t.''   [E. dial., perhaps for *''brine'', < ''brīne'', orig. a burning. Cf. ''brin''<sup>1</sup>, var. of ''burn''<sup>1</sup>.]   To keep fire at the mouth of (an oven), either to give light or preserve the heat. [North. Eng.]

'''briar, briary''', etc. See ''brier'', ''briery'', etc.

'''briarbot''' (brī′är-bot), ''n.''   [< ''briar'', ''brier'', + (appar.) ''bot'', a var. of ''but''<sup>2</sup>.]   A local Irish name of the fish called the angler. Several brier-like protuberances arm the head.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
